name: Dark umber
lede: Dark umber is a near-black, faintly red-brown shade of umber, the old earth pigment; our data files this exact English name as the gloss for a Japanese traditional color, Fujisusutake.

sections.title: An old pigment, a newer gloss
sections.body: The base word, [[umber]], is the manganese-rich brown earth that European painters took up in the late 1400s [4]. Some writers derive its name from Umbria, but Ball and other books lean toward the Latin for shadow, noting the earth came mostly from Turkey [4]. Our data files Dark umber itself only through the Japanese traditional color list, as the English rendering of *Fujisusutake* (藤煤竹), "wisteria and burnt bamboo," rather than through a Western pigment catalog [1]. No Ridgway plate or ISCC-NBS block is given for this exact darkened name in our sources [1]. Its nearest named neighbors on file are [[chocolate-red]] and [[deep-reddish-brown]], at 2.7 and 3.3 CIEDE2000 units, both redder than this near-black brown [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this near-black brown, as photographed, in 448 of 23,781 paintings, 1.88 percent, more common than 75 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, 49 of 1,674 paintings from that century, 2.7 times the expected rate [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a mid-tone, in 43 percent of the 298 paintings our within-painting lens counts [3]. It shares canvases with Hay's Brown and Black Blue more than chance would predict [3].
